13.8.7 The USSD 2025 TiP report stated: ‘… [O]bservers reported NAPTIP lacked sufficient resources to fully execute its broad mandate. The anti-trafficking law called for a NAPTIP board, including two civil society representatives; however, the government has never appointed a board.’[footnote 254]

13.8.8 The USSD 2025 TiP report stated:

‘Corruption and official complicity in trafficking crimes, including among designated officials with responsibilities to combat human trafficking, remained significant concerns, inhibiting law enforcement action and perpetuating impunity for trafficking crimes. The government initiated prosecution of one National Immigration Services (NIS) official for sex trafficking crimes, compared with prosecuting and convicting three complicit officials during the previous year [2024][footnote 255]. Prosecutions of one Civilian Joint Task Force member for alleged sex trafficking remained pending. During the previous reporting period, NAPTIP fired five staff members, including a deputy director, and demoted three staff members for complicity in trafficking crimes, including soliciting bribes and leaking confidential information to trafficking suspects; however, the government did not report initiating any prosecutions of the officials. Observers reported some law enforcement, military, and other government officials reportedly committed trafficking crimes, accepted bribes to facilitate trafficking, or obstructed justice by interfering with investigations. Endemic judicial corruption impeded prosecutions and convictions of most crimes, including human trafficking. Observers previously reported some security officers sexually abused and exploited IDPs, including children, in and around Maiduguri (the Borno State capital).’[footnote 256]

13.8.9 The same USSD report also stated: ‘The government provided victim-witnesses assistance, including security, victim advocates, temporary immigration relief, and travel and lodging.’[footnote 257]

13.8.10 The USSD 2025 TiP report did not state how many victims, if any, received such services. However, the USSD 2023 TiP report, dated 15 June 2023, stated that the government reported 60 victims had participated in criminal justice proceedings and received services. The USSD 2024 TiP report, dated 24 June 2024, observed that the government reported 40 victims had done so[footnote 258].

13.8.11 The USSD 2025 TiP report further stated:

‘[The government] also provided victims a six-week recovery and reflection period to decide whether to cooperate with law enforcement proceedings. Victims were able to testify in the judges’ private chambers to protect their privacy and safety, and courts sometimes used video testimony. NAPTIP, in collaboration with an international organization, the MOJ, and NGOs, ran legal hubs in Edo, Delta, and Lagos states, intended to improve victims’ access to justice through legal aid counseling and representation in court … [T]he government did not report utilizing the [victim trust] fund to support victims, and observers reported it was not operational. [C]ourts awarded [victim] restitution in two cases … [T]he government did not report whether any victims [filed civil suits against their traffickers].’[footnote 259]

13.8.12 For more information on the victim trust fund, victim restitution and civil suits, see Law and policy measures.

13.8.13 According to the USSD 2025 TiP report, although the High Courts had jurisdiction over trafficking cases, ‘in practice, cases were sometimes tried in state courts, which heard lower-level or misdemeanor crimes. Local judges did not have the same standardized training requirements as federal and state judges, which contributed to corruption and misapplication of the law. Illegal activities of non-state armed groups hindered law enforcement efforts, especially in northern Nigeria.’[footnote 260]

13.8.14 The same USSD report further stated:

‘The government, in collaboration with foreign donors and civil society, provided anti-trafficking training to law enforcement officials, security forces, and service providers. Observers reported law enforcement investigators required additional resources and training on investigative techniques, cybercrime, and financial crimes. The government did not report holding any anti-trafficking trainings for prosecutors or judges, and observers reported a lack of judicial training and awareness of the anti-trafficking law impeded prosecutions. NAPTIP’s Judicial Research Center in Abuja provided NAPTIP officers access to resources to strengthen trafficking cases and support prosecution efforts.’[footnote 261]

13.8.15 According to the same USSD report, ‘… [B]oth informal and registered recruitment agents continued fraudulently recruiting and exploiting victims; despite reporting that such practices remained prevalent, officials did not report initiating any investigations into fraudulent recruitment or revoking any licenses for exploitative recruitment practices.’[footnote 262]

13.8.16 The 2025 EUAA report stated: ‘According to [IRARA director] Roland Nwoha, NAPTIP tends to operate more reactively than proactively, often waiting for complaints before acting. Its effectiveness is further constrained by inadequate funding … Sources also indicated that corruption has hindered investigations and prosecutions of traffickers. [WOCON director Morenike Omaiboje] noted that court proceedings are often slow, with few successful prosecutions. Access to justice and convictions remain major challenges, largely due to poor implementation and corruption, despite existing legal structures and a trained judiciary …

9.2.2 The same ENACT report observed that online recruitment of victims has been increasing, adding: ‘According to Europol, “most victims are identified and recruited via the Internet, particularly on social media platforms”.’[footnote 51] Offline recruitment ‘generally takes place through intermediaries … Nigerian women are also often recruited at markets or shops.’[footnote 52]

9.2.3 The 2024 Punch roles article reported: ‘… Throughout the entirety of the trafficking chain, spanning from the initial referrer to the Connection Man, Buyer, and ultimately the User, devious tactics are employed to keep the victims unaware of the imminent danger they are facing.’[footnote 53]

9.2.4 The 2024 UNODC global trafficking report stated: ‘Working on or with family members is a tactical strategy used by traffickers who understand the key aspects of respecting and obeying elders in the Nigerian society, and use that to their advantage.’[footnote 54]

9.2.5 The USSD 2025 TiP report observed:

‘Traffickers increasingly use social media to identify and recruit potential victims. Media and NGOs report unscrupulous actors, including Russian officials and illicit recruiters, fraudulently recruited women ages 18-22 from Africa – including Nigeria – … for vocational training programs and subsequently placed them in military drone production sites. Media report workers at these sites are subjected to hazardous conditions, surveillance, hour and wage violations, contract switching, and worker-paid recruitment fees, all of which are indicators of human trafficking.’[footnote 55]

9.2.6 According to the 2025 ENACT report: ‘Sex trafficking Nigerian criminal confraternities [cults] such as the Black Axe, Supreme Viking Confraternity, Arobaga Vikings, the Maphite, and the Eiye syndicate are becoming more organized, violent, and sophisticated. They also collaborate with European mafia and OCGs and are diversifying their criminal activities while focusing less on human trafficking.’[footnote 56]

9.2.7 El País, a Madrid-based[footnote 57] media outlet owned by PRISA Media[footnote 58], published an article in Spanish on 29 July 2025 that has been translated for this note using an online translation tool. The article reported:

‘Human traffickers are rarely strangers who approach their victims and take them away by force. Fatima Waziri-Azi, an expert on human trafficking and former director general of the National Agency for the Prohibition of Trafficking in Persons (NAPTIP), says that traffickers often approach young women with seemingly legitimate, well-paid job offers such as domestic workers, models, caregivers, or hospitality workers. In some cases, they are even promised scholarships or vocational training opportunities in Europe, the Middle East or other African countries …

‘“Young women are often under enormous pressure to provide for their families or to escape an abusive environment. That pressure makes them more likely to take risks, especially when someone they trust offers them a way out. In the internet age in which we live, traffickers skillfully manipulate the stories found online, idealizing life abroad,” explains the expert.’[footnote 59]

9.2.8 For more information, see Profile of victims of trafficking.

9.2.9 In relation to baby factories, the 2025 EUAA report stated: ‘Victims often receive money or something else for giving birth to a child. In some cases, families facilitate the involvement of girls, while in other cases victims themselves engage voluntarily for financial reasons. Some victims of so-called “baby-factories” are recruited by traffickers through online platforms.’[footnote 60]

9.2.10 Regarding new trafficking types and methods, Sahara Reporters, ‘an online community of international reporters and social advocates’[footnote 61], in an article dated 24 July 2025, reported:

‘The Director-General [DG] of Nigeria’s National Agency for the Prohibition of Trafficking in Persons and other related offences (NAPTIP), Binta Adamu Bello, has raised the alarm over a series of emerging and disturbing trends in human trafficking in Nigeria and Ghana.

‘[Emerging patterns of exploitation] include organ harvesting, where victims, often lured with false promises, are trafficked for the illicit trade of human organs …

‘“Online sextortion and revenge porn, where youths are increasingly falling victim to digital exploitation, particularly in Nigeria and Ghana. Loan-for-sex trafficking schemes, where criminals now use fake online loan offers to trap women into prostitution in exchange for debt repayment. Fake job offers and scholarships, where traffickers pose as employers or scholarship agents to lure unsuspecting individuals abroad, only to exploit them. Recruitment for cybercrime …, where young people, especially in Nigeria and Ghana, are being trafficked into online scams … Recruitment as ‘Marketing Agents’, where some victims are deceived into working as agents for branded products but are later exploited. These criminal networks are driving victimisation using migration flows, digital platforms, legal and economic loopholes to facilitate cross-border trafficking at a massive scale,” Bello said.’[footnote 62]

passages.quote:
Version 7.0, October 2026

Executive summary

Women victims of trafficking from Nigeria form a particular social group (PSG).

In general, a woman who has previously been trafficked is unlikely to be at risk of abuse, reprisals and/or discrimination on return that are sufficiently serious by their nature or repetition to amount to persecution or serious harm, solely on account of having previously been trafficked.

In general, a woman is unlikely to be at real risk of being re-trafficked on return solely on account of having previously been trafficked.

However, a woman may be at risk of abuse and/or re-trafficking amounting to persecution or serious harm depending on her particular circumstances and vulnerability. Factors which may increase vulnerability include, but are not limited to:

outstanding debts owed to traffickers or others who financed the journey

family or community involvement in the trafficking

the absence of a supportive family or social support network

social stigma or family rejection

poverty, destitution or lack of sustainable income

limited education, vocational skills or employment opportunities

mental health conditions or psychological trauma arising from trafficking experiences

In general, a victim of trafficking who has a well-founded fear of persecution or serious harm from a rogue state actor and/or a non-state actor is likely to be able to obtain protection from the state. However, the effectiveness of protection remains uneven. Corruption, official complicity in trafficking offences, inadequate funding, weaknesses in victim identification, limited shelter capacity and shortcomings within the criminal justice system may hamper protection in some cases. The onus is on the person to demonstrate that they cannot obtain protection.

Where a woman has a well-founded fear of persecution as a victim of trafficking, whether she is able to relocate to escape that risk depends on her particular circumstances. In the country guidance case of HD (Trafficked women) Nigeria (CG) [2016] UKUT 454 (IAC), heard 18 to 20 July 2016 and promulgated 17 October 2016, the Upper Tribunal held that a woman who discloses characteristics of vulnerability that are indicative of a real risk of being trafficked, internal relocation is unlikely to be a viable alternative. There are not very strong grounds supported by cogent evidence to justify a departure from these findings. The onus is on decision makers to demonstrate that internal relocation is reasonable (or not unduly harsh) having regard to the individual circumstances of the person.

Where a claim is refused, it is unlikely to be certifiable as ‘clearly unfounded’ under section 94 of the Nationality, Immigration and Asylum Act 2002.

Each case must be considered on its individual facts, with the onus on the person to demonstrate they face persecution or serious harm.

Assessment

Section updated: 07 September 2026

About the assessment

This section considers relevant evidence – including country information, refugee and human rights laws and policies, and case law – to assess whether, in general:

a person faces a real risk of persecution/serious harm by non-state actors because they are a victim of trafficking

the state (or quasi state bodies) can provide effective protection

internal relocation is possible to avoid persecution/serious harm

a claim, if refused, it is unlikely to be certified as ‘clearly unfounded’ under section 94 of the Nationality, Immigration and Asylum Act 2002.

Each case must be considered on its individual facts.

For details on how CPIT makes its assessments, gathers and presents country information, its research methodology and disclaimers and explainers on coverage, source selection, maps, translations and the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in developing CPIT products, see About country policy and information notes.

1. Material facts, credibility and other checks

1.1.1 Decision makers must:

assess credibility (see the Asylum Instruction on Assessing Credibility and Refugee Status

check if there has been a previous application for a UK visa or another form of leave. Asylum applications matched to visas should be investigated prior to the asylum interview (see the Asylum Instruction on Visa Matches, Asylum Claims from UK Visa Applicants).

consider making an international biometric data-sharing check, when one has not already been undertaken (see Biometric data-sharing process (Migration 5 biometric data-sharing process)).

consider language analysis testing, where available, in cases where there are doubts surrounding a person’s claimed place of origin (see the Asylum Instruction on Language Analysis).

1.2 Modern slavery

1.2.1 Decision makers must note that guidance for competent authority staff in any part of the UK who make decisions on whether or not a person is a potential victim/victim of modern slavery for the purpose of the National Referral Mechanism is set out in the Modern Slavery: Statutory Guidance for England and Wales (under s49 of the Modern Slavery Act 2015) and non-statutory guidance for Scotland and Northern Ireland. The guidance is also aimed at staff within public authorities who may encounter potential victims of modern slavery and/or who are involved in supporting victims.

1.2.2 Decision makers also must note that if a person has a ‘positive conclusive grounds’ decision, a grant of permission to stay as a victim of human trafficking or slavery by the competent authorities may be considered.

1.2.3 For further information, see Temporary permission to stay for victims of human trafficking or slavery.
